articles.title: Smaller EV batteries, longer range? Scientists may have found a way
articles.summary: Scientists have developed a new technology that could make electric vehicle batteries smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting, potentially allowing cars to travel farther on a single charge. By borrowing precision manufacturing techniques from computer chip production, they found a way to prevent damaging lithium buildup that has held back next-generation batteries.
articles.content:
Researchers in South Korea have developed a new technology that could lead to smaller, lighter electric vehicle (EV) batteries capable of delivering longer driving ranges on a single charge. Scientists at KAIST have found a way to address a major weakness of anode-free batteries, which eliminate conventional materials such as graphite to reduce battery size and weight. Although these batteries can store more energy in less space, their lifespan is often limited by the formation of sharp lithium structures during charging. The researchers tackled this problem by adapting precision manufacturing techniques from the semiconductor industry, allowing lithium to accumulate more evenly while encouraging the development of a durable protective layer.

On September 22, KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) announced the breakthrough by a collaborative team led by Professors Jinwoo Lee and Hee-Tae Jung of its Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering. The project also involved scientists from Kyungpook National University (President Heo Young-woo) and the National NanoFab Center (President Park Heung Soo). By applying extremely precise fabrication methods traditionally used to manufacture semiconductor devices, the researchers developed an approach that extends the operating life of anode-free batteries without significantly increasing their size or weight.

Why Anode-Free Batteries Could Transform Electric Vehicles

In conventional lithium-ion batteries, lithium is stored in an anode made from materials such as graphite when the battery charges. Anode-free batteries operate differently. Instead of relying on a separate anode material, they allow lithium to accumulate directly on a thin sheet of copper foil.

Removing the conventional anode eliminates material that would otherwise contribute to the battery's overall weight and thickness. This makes it possible to store more energy within the same amount of space, potentially allowing electric vehicles to travel farther without requiring larger or heavier battery packs.

However, this promising design comes with a serious drawback. As the battery repeatedly charges and discharges, lithium does not always spread evenly across the copper surface. Instead, it can accumulate in branching or needle-like formations called dendrites.

These structures interfere with battery performance, while the protective layer surrounding the lithium can also become unstable. Together, these problems cause the battery to deteriorate more quickly, making limited lifespan one of the biggest barriers to bringing anode-free batteries into widespread commercial use.

Previous attempts to address this issue have included supplying additional lithium to replace material lost during operation or covering the electrode with a thicker protective coating. Although these approaches can help compensate for degradation or shield the surface, they also introduce additional material. The resulting increase in thickness and weight undermines the main advantage of anode-free battery technology.

Borrowing Semiconductor Technology To Prevent Lithium Spikes

Rather than adding substantial amounts of material, the KAIST-led team focused on changing the structure of the copper foil where lithium accumulates.

The researchers created a carefully arranged pattern of microscopic tubes across the copper surface. The concept resembles dividing a large parking lot into many individual spaces. Instead of allowing lithium to collect unevenly in certain areas, the tiny structures provide a more uniform distribution of locations where it can settle.

To produce these features, the team adapted a semiconductor manufacturing technique known as secondary sputtering lithography (SSL). This process makes it possible to fabricate extremely small structures with high precision.

Each tube measured approximately 300 nanometers across and 150 nanometers tall. Despite their tiny dimensions, the structures increased the copper foil's available surface area for lithium deposition to roughly four times that of an ordinary flat sheet.

The expanded surface helps distribute lithium more evenly, reducing the concentrated buildup that can lead to damaging spikes. This approach improves the conditions for stable lithium deposition without relying on large amounts of additional material.

An Ultrathin Protective Coating Helps Batteries Last Longer

The researchers went a step further by applying a coating of MXene, a two-dimensional material, to the copper foil. The coating was approximately 10 nanometers thick, equivalent to only a few thousandths of the thickness of a human hair.

Instead of functioning as the battery's final protective barrier, the MXene acts as a foundation that encourages a stronger protective layer to develop during operation. Much like a primer prepares a surface for paint, it helps bring together the ingredients needed to create a stable coating.

In the LiPF6-based electrolyte used in the experiments, the MXene surface promotes the formation of a protective layer containing high concentrations of lithium fluoride (LiF).

This layer helps limit unwanted chemical reactions between the lithium and the electrolyte while also restricting the growth of damaging lithium spikes. By stabilizing the electrode surface, it addresses two important causes of deterioration in anode-free batteries.

To understand how the protective layer develops, the scientists examined the electrode surfaces and internal cross sections while carefully limiting their exposure to air. Their observations confirmed that a nanoscale protective layer forms evenly along the MXene surface and helped explain the process responsible for its formation.

The investigation involved several advanced analytical methods, including X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).

A Promising Step Toward Smaller, Longer-Lasting EV Batteries

Professor Jinwoo Lee said, "This study shows how ultrafine fabrication techniques used in semiconductor manufacturing can create both uniform sites for lithium deposition and a stable protective layer without changing the bulk electrolyte formulation or adding excess lithium."

He also explained that the findings could help accelerate the commercial development of high-energy anode-free batteries. By improving battery lifespan while keeping additional weight and volume to a minimum, the technology could support the development of more compact energy storage systems for future electric vehicles.

KAIST researchers Eunji Kim, Hyunju Jung, and Jinuk Kim served as co-first authors of the study. The findings were published online on September 1 in the international journal Advanced Functional Materials.

The research received funding from the Nano&Material Technology Development Program through the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), supported by the Ministry of Science and ICT (RS-2026-25542167). Additional support came from the Global Semiconductor Advanced Fab Utilization Project through the National Nano Fab Center (NNFC) and the Semiconductor-Secondary Battery Interfacing Platform Technology Development Project of NNFC.

articles.personality_title: New battery design could make electric vehicles lighter and travel farther
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Electric vehicles (EVs) use batteries that store energy to power the car. A big challenge is making these batteries smaller and lighter while still lasting a long time and allowing cars to drive far on one charge.

**What happened** – Scientists in South Korea, led by KAIST, developed a new technology that changes the surface of the battery’s copper part using tiny tubes made with methods from making computer chips. This helps lithium spread more evenly inside the battery, stopping sharp lithium growths that damage it. They also added a very thin coating called MXene that helps form a strong protective layer. This means the battery can last longer without getting heavier or bigger.

**Impact** – This is important because it solves a big problem with a type of battery called anode-free batteries. These batteries can store more energy in less space but usually wear out quickly because lithium builds up unevenly. The new method keeps the battery light and small while making it last longer. This could help make electric cars that are easier to build and can drive further without bigger batteries.

**What's next step** – The researchers hope this technology will speed up making better anode-free batteries for real electric cars. More testing and development will follow to bring these improved batteries to the market, possibly changing how EVs are powered in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using tiny structures and a special coating, scientists created a new battery design that helps electric cars drive farther with smaller, lighter batteries.

articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo diseño de batería podría hacer que los vehículos eléctricos sean más ligeros y recorran más distancia
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los vehículos eléctricos (VE) usan baterías para almacenar energía y mover el auto. Un gran reto es hacer estas baterías más pequeñas y ligeras, pero que duren mucho tiempo y permitan recorrer más kilómetros con una sola carga.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos en Corea del Sur, liderados por KAIST, desarrollaron una tecnología que cambia la superficie de cobre de la batería con tubos muy pequeños hechos con técnicas de fabricación de chips de computadora. Esto ayuda a que el litio se distribuya de manera más uniforme dentro de la batería, evitando que crezcan puntas que la dañan. Además, aplicaron un recubrimiento muy delgado llamado MXene que ayuda a crear una capa protectora fuerte. Esto permite que la batería dure más sin volverse más pesada o grande.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque resuelve un problema grande de las baterías llamadas sin ánodo. Estas baterías pueden guardar más energía en menos espacio, pero suelen dañarse rápido porque el litio no se distribuye bien. El nuevo método mantiene la batería ligera y pequeña, pero hace que dure más. Esto podría ayudar a fabricar autos eléctricos más fáciles de construir y que puedan recorrer más distancia sin baterías más grandes.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores esperan que esta tecnología acelere la creación de mejores baterías sin ánodo para autos eléctricos reales. Se harán más pruebas y desarrollos para llevar estas baterías mejoradas al mercado, lo que podría cambiar cómo se alimentan los VE en el futuro.

**Frase clave** – Usando estructuras diminutas y un recubrimiento especial, científicos crearon un nuevo diseño de batería que ayuda a que los autos eléctricos recorran más distancia con baterías más pequeñas y ligeras.

articles.title: Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics
articles.summary: Scientists have defied a long-standing rule of laser physics by generating X-rays with much higher energies than conventional theory predicts. The surprising discovery reveals how two electrons working together can overcome a previously accepted limit, opening new possibilities for quantum research.
articles.content:
Scientists have pushed X-ray generation beyond a long-accepted limit in laser physics, revealing a surprising quantum effect that conventional theory does not account for. By directing powerful ultraviolet lasers at helium atoms, researchers produced X-rays with substantially higher energies than the standard model predicts. The breakthrough depends on an unusual interaction between two electrons that allows them to release their energy together.

The discovery comes from a collaboration between TU Wien and the University of California San Diego and builds on research that helped establish the field of attosecond physics. Laser techniques developed at TU Wien in the 1990s contributed to advances recognized by the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics.

For decades, scientists have understood that directing laser light at certain atoms can cause them to emit extremely short pulses of much higher-frequency light, including X-rays. However, the established theory predicts a maximum energy for these emissions based on the properties of the incoming laser. Beyond this boundary, known as the energy cutoff, X-ray production becomes extremely weak.

The new experiment demonstrates that this familiar limit can be exceeded when two electrons interact in a particular way. The findings were published in Nature Photonics.

How Lasers Generate Powerful X-Ray Pulses

"The mechanism behind short X-ray pulses has been well known for a long time," says Prof. Tenio Popmintchev from the Institute of Photonics at TU Wien. "The laser tears a single electron away from the atom. The electron is then accelerated in the laser's electric field until it eventually collides with the atom again. The energy it loses in the process is emitted in the form of light."

During this process, the laser's electric field drives the freed electron away from its parent atom before bringing it back. When the electron returns and releases its energy, it generates light at frequencies far higher than those of the original laser beam.

Nobel laureate Ferenc Krausz used this mechanism in pioneering experiments during the 1990s. Tenio Popmintchev and his colleagues now work at the same TU Wien institute where Krausz conducted his earlier research, but their latest experiment has pushed the process beyond its previously understood boundaries.

"It can be shown that when the electron returns to its atom, it generates a whole range of different frequencies with roughly equal intensity," says Dimitar Popmintchev, postdoc in Tenio Popmintchev's team at TU Wien. "But there is an upper limit. Frequencies above this limit are much weaker; it is simply not possible to exceed a certain maximum frequency."

That prediction describes the conventional process involving a single electron. The researchers wanted to find out whether the outcome would change if two electrons participated instead.

Two Electrons Break the Expected X-Ray Energy Limit

To investigate, the team used intense ultraviolet (UV) laser pulses to interact with helium atoms. Unlike the usual process involving one electron, the experiment allowed both of helium's electrons to be removed in succession.

The first electron was released and accelerated by the laser field, followed by the second. Although the electrons were freed at different moments, their behavior remained connected through quantum correlations. This relationship means their motions cannot be treated as entirely independent.

By carefully controlling the ultraviolet laser pulses, the researchers could arrange for both electrons to return to the atom simultaneously.

"Using UV driving pulses, we can arrange for both electrons to return to the atom at exactly the same time," says Dimitar Popmintchev. "The energy of two electrons is then released all at once. And when more energy is available, a single higher-energy X-ray photon with higher frequency can also be generated."

This coordinated release of energy makes it possible to produce X-ray photons that exceed the conventional energy cutoff. Rather than relying on the energy of a single returning electron, the process draws on the combined energy of two interacting electrons.

An Unexpected X-Ray Signal Confirms the Discovery

The researchers found clear experimental evidence that the two-electron process was producing unusually energetic X-rays.

When they examined the spectrum of the emitted coherent radiation, they identified a second region of sustained emission at much higher photon energies than the standard theory predicts. This additional region, known as a plateau, was weaker than the primary emission but extended well beyond the previously established energy range.

The unexpected signal appeared only when the researchers used helium. Similar experiments involving argon and neon did not produce the same behavior in their outer electrons.

This difference provides important evidence for the proposed explanation. Helium has particularly strong correlations between its two electrons, allowing them to interact in ways that make the simultaneous release of energy possible. The outer electrons of argon and neon did not demonstrate the same effect under the experimental conditions.

A New Window Into Quantum Physics

Beyond producing higher-energy X-rays, the discovery could give scientists a powerful new way to investigate how electrons interact inside atoms and other materials.

The unusual coherent X-ray emission could serve as a highly sensitive spectroscopic "sensor" for electron-electron correlations. By studying the shape of the emitted spectrum, its maximum energy, and how it changes with the polarization of the laser light, researchers could gain information about the behavior of interacting electrons on extraordinarily short timescales.

These interactions occur over attoseconds, with one attosecond equal to one billionth of a billionth of a second. Observing processes at such speeds is essential for understanding how electrons move and influence one another in quantum systems.

Eventually, the same principle might be extended beyond individual helium atoms to molecules and solid materials in which electrons interact strongly.

The technique behind the discovery, known as high-harmonic generation, originally helped make attosecond physics possible. Now, researchers are finding that it can also reveal the complex behavior of multiple interacting quantum particles.

These insights could contribute to research on quantum computing and help scientists understand and design advanced nanomaterials with carefully controlled properties.

articles.title: NASA University Challenge Ignites Trajectory of Drone Entrepreneur
articles.summary: Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge. Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students […]
articles.content:
Four co-founders of AG3 Labs –from left Matt Atkinson, Gavin Gardner, Ryan Atkinson, and Gryson Gardner – show off the military training drones their company builds at a U.S. Army event at Camp Grayling in Michigan. As a student, Gavin was on a Michigan State team twice selected for participation in NASA’s University Student Research Challenge. His NASA experience served as a foundation for the creation of AG3. AG3 Labs

Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge.

Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students in a lab setting, he and his team were completely new to things like creating budgets, handling large sums of money, and promoting their work for crowdfunding.

That’s why demonstrating both engineering and entrepreneurship skills are major tentpoles of NASA’s University Student Research Challenge (USRC), an initiative that provides grants to teams of college students interested in helping the agency realize its aeronautical research goals.

“Half the battle is building your product,” Gardner said recently. “The other half is selling the product in a way that everyone else can understand what you’re doing and not talking in nerdy, engineering ways.”

We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers. STEVEN HOLZ NASA USRC Manager

Gardner and his Michigan State USRC alumni teammates are still using those lessons today, as aerospace developers. In 2024, they founded their own company, AG3 Labs, which specializes in drones for military training exercises.

“I don’t think I would discredit our technical expertise in getting us to where we are today, but I know that USRC was a booster that really amplified our trajectory at such a young age,” Gardner said.

NASA USRC manager Steven Holz said Gardner’s experience shows what students can accomplish when they receive both a grant and guidance – enabling a future workforce and contributing to the aviation industry.

“We are proud to see the success of USRC alumni,” Holz said. “We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers.”

Research path

Gardner’s path to running his own company began with a middle school age trip to Space Camp, where he began realizing that he wanted to be an engineer.

The engineering bug also bit his brother, Gryson Gardner, and the two of them would often be found in their Michigan garage tinkering with various machinery, including drones and electronic kits.

When Gardner arrived at Michigan State, he looked for extracurricular groups and found one dedicated to the increasingly popular hobby of drones. He gained hands-on, practical experience in how drones are made and operated.

In 2021, Gardner received an email from a friend who told him they had just won a USRC grant from NASA for an activity called Aerial Intra-city Delivery Electric Drones (AIDED), and they needed help building a new drone.

“We had this idea that instead of flying through the whole city, why can’t a drone just hitchhike a ride on a city bus like everyone else does?” Gardner said.

The concept was for a cargo-carrying drone to take off, dock on top of public transportation such as a bus, charge its batteries while riding along, and then take off for its final leg of the delivery. The team built and flew a full-scale drone to prove the concept but decided against pursuing a commercial venture.

“The commercial drone market kind of scared us a little bit with the large number of regulations that go into operating such a novel idea like this with flying over people in a dense city,” Gardner said.

But the team’s demonstration of technical prowess and confidence led to a second USRC award from NASA in 2023 – the Laser Energized Aerial Drone System (LEADS), which focused on using a laser to transfer power directly to a drone in flight.

While working on LEADS, which led to flying a prototype, Gardner’s network of contacts within the drone community expanded to include NASA personnel at the Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, who made him aware of internship opportunities, which he applied for and was accepted while in graduate school.

Gavin Gardner, a University Student Research Challenge participant who went on to co-found his own drone company, also was a NASA intern in 2024 and wrote this social media post.

Student challenge paves way for opportunity

As his graduation in the spring of 2025 with a master’s degree approached, Gardner took the initial steps in late 2024 to co-found with his brother and other USRC alumni AG3 Labs after a friend suggested the military could use low-cost drones to test effective counter drone systems.

An initial award from the U.S. Army led to more contracts, allowing the company to expand and ramp up its operations, where today their production capability enables thousands of drones to be built each month.

Gardner credits his experience with USRC, especially when it came to learning more about the business side of running a technical operation, with helping create the opportunities for success he and his team are experiencing today.

articles.personality_title_fr: Le défi étudiant de la NASA lance une entreprise de drones prospère
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Il y a cinq ans, Gavin Gardner était étudiant en ingénierie à l’Université d’État du Michigan. Il a participé à un programme de la NASA appelé University Student Research Challenge (USRC), qui soutient des équipes universitaires travaillant sur de nouvelles technologies de drones.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Gavin et ses coéquipiers ont reçu deux fois des subventions de la NASA pour développer des idées innovantes de drones. Leurs projets comprenaient un drone pouvant se déplacer sur des bus en ville pour économiser la batterie et un drone alimenté par un laser en vol. articles.personality_title: Scientists grow ancient microbes that reveal how complex cells evolved
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long studied how complex cells, like those in animals and plants, first appeared. These cells have parts inside them called organelles, which simpler cells do not have. Archaea are a group of tiny living things that are different from bacteria and may be related to the ancestors of these complex cells.

**What happened** – Researchers successfully grew two types of archaea in the lab. These archaea belong to a group that is closely connected to the ancient ancestor of complex cells, also called eukaryotic cells. By studying their simple insides, surface shapes, partnerships with other microbes, and how they live using proteins, scientists gained new clues about how complex cells might have started.

**Impact** – This is important because it helps explain one of the biggest questions in biology: how did cells with organelles evolve from simpler cells? The discovery shows details about the step-by-step changes that led to complex life forms, improving our understanding of evolution and life on Earth.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue to study these archaea to learn more about their biology and how they interact with other organisms. This may lead to new discoveries about cell evolution and could also influence fields like medicine and environmental science.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Growing ancient archaea in the lab gives scientists new information about how complex cells, like those in plants and animals, first evolved.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des microbes anciens cultivés en laboratoire révèlent l’évolution des cellules complexes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques cherchent depuis longtemps à comprendre comment sont apparues les cellules complexes, comme celles des animaux et des plantes. Ces cellules ont des parties à l’intérieur appelées organites, que les cellules plus simples n’ont pas. Les archées sont un groupe de petits êtres vivants différents des bactéries et proches des ancêtres des cellules complexes.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs ont réussi à cultiver en laboratoire deux types d’archées. Ces archées appartiennent à un groupe lié à l’ancêtre ancien des cellules complexes, appelées cellules eucaryotes. En étudiant leur organisation simple, leurs formes extérieures, leurs relations avec d’autres microbes et leur mode de vie basé sur des protéines, les scientifiques ont trouvé de nouveaux indices sur l’origine des cellules complexes.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle aide à comprendre une grande question de la biologie : comment les cellules avec organites ont-elles évolué à partir de cellules plus simples ? Elle montre les étapes qui ont mené à la vie complexe et améliore notre compréhension de l’évolution et de la vie sur Terre.

**Étape suivante** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à étudier ces archées pour mieux comprendre leur biologie et leurs interactions. Cela pourrait conduire à de nouvelles découvertes sur l’évolution cellulaire et avoir des applications en médecine ou en environnement.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Cultiver des archées anciennes en laboratoire offre aux scientifiques de nouvelles informations sur l’évolution des cellules complexes, comme celles des plantes et des animaux.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos cultivan microbios antiguos que revelan cómo evolucionaron las células complejas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han estudiado durante mucho tiempo cómo aparecieron las células complejas, como las de animales y plantas. Estas células tienen partes internas llamadas orgánulos, que las células más simples no tienen. Las arqueas son un grupo de seres vivos muy pequeños, diferentes de las bacterias, y están relacionadas con los ancestros de estas células complejas.

**Qué pasó** – Los investigadores lograron cultivar en el laboratorio dos tipos de arqueas. Estas arqueas pertenecen a un grupo muy cercano al ancestro antiguo de las células complejas, llamadas células eucariotas. Al estudiar su estructura simple, sus formas externas, sus relaciones con otros microbios y su forma de vida dependiente de proteínas, los científicos encontraron nuevas pistas sobre cómo surgieron las células complejas.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque ayuda a responder una gran pregunta en biología: ¿cómo evolucionaron las células con orgánulos a partir de células más simples? Este descubrimiento muestra detalles sobre los pasos que llevaron a la vida compleja y mejora nuestro entendimiento de la evolución y la vida en la Tierra.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán estudiando estas arqueas para aprender más sobre su biología y cómo interactúan con otros organismos. Esto podría llevar a nuevos descubrimientos sobre la evolución celular y también influir en áreas como la medicina y la ciencia ambiental.

**Resumen en una frase** – Cultivar arqueas antiguas en el laboratorio da nueva información a los científicos sobre cómo evolucionaron las células complejas, como las de plantas y animales.
